title: What are unit economics, and how do you use them in a case?
description: What unit economics means, how to work out the profit on one order, customer or store, and why it is often the fastest way into a case.
hook: Unit economics means working out whether a business makes money on one unit (one order, one customer, one store, one flight) before worrying about the whole company. In a case, it is often the fastest way to the answer: if a single unit loses money, growing faster only loses money faster, and if it makes money, the question becomes whether there are enough units to cover fixed costs.
body:
What counts as a unit?

Whatever the business sells or repeats, and whatever its decisions are made around. For a delivery app it is one order. For a gym or a software company it is one customer. For a coffee chain it is usually one store. For an airline, one flight. Pick the unit that matches the question: "Should we offer bigger first-order discounts?" is about customers; "Should we close this branch?" is about stores.

A worked example: one food delivery order

An illustrative delivery app:

LinePer order
Commission: 25% of a $25 order$6.25
Delivery fee paid by the customer$2.00
Revenue per order$8.25
Rider pay−$4.50
Card fees−$0.40
Customer support and refunds−$0.60
Discounts and vouchers−$1.50
Contribution per order$1.25

The big-picture questions now become easy to frame. With $1.25 per order, the app needs $1M ÷ $1.25 = 800,000 orders a month just to cover $1M of monthly fixed costs such as offices and engineers. At 1.6M orders it makes $1M a month; at 400,000 it loses $500k.

When scale helps, and when it doesn't

Scale helps when each unit makes money: fixed costs are spread over more orders and profit rises. But suppose management chases growth with bigger vouchers, adding $1.50 per order. Contribution becomes $1.25 − $1.50 = −$0.25. Now every extra order deepens the loss, and doubling volume doubles the damage. Growth only helps when unit economics are positive, or will reliably become positive.

Unit economics for customers: LTV and CAC

When the unit is a customer, two numbers matter. LTV (lifetime value) is the contribution a customer brings over the whole time they stay. CAC (customer acquisition cost) is what it costs to win them. A commonly quoted rule of thumb is that LTV should be at least three times CAC.

Continue the delivery example. A typical customer orders twice a month, so brings 2 × $1.25 = $2.50 a month. If 5% of customers stop ordering each month, the average customer stays 1 ÷ 0.05 = 20 months, so LTV ≈ $2.50 × 20 = $50. If winning a customer costs $30 in ads and first-order vouchers, LTV is only 1.7 times CAC. The business needs higher contribution per order, more orders per customer, lower churn or cheaper acquisition.

Units with fixed costs: the store

For chains, the unit is often a store, and it has fixed costs of its own (rent, staff) as well as a share of central costs. A store can cover its own costs but look unprofitable after central overhead is allocated to it. Closing it would not remove that overhead, so judge each store on what it contributes before allocations. The third practice question works through one.

Why interviewers like it

It shows you can cut through a big, messy problem. Saying "Before looking at the whole company, I'd like to understand the profit on a single order" signals clear thinking, and it often finds the answer quickly.

Weak: "The company is losing money, so it needs to grow revenue."
Strong: "Let me first check whether each order makes money on its own. If it doesn't, growth won't fix the problem; if it does, the question is how many orders we need to cover fixed costs."

Common mistakes

  • Leaving costs out of the unit. Discounts, refunds and support are real per-order costs. Some reported "contribution" figures quietly exclude them.
  • Mixing time periods. Do not divide a yearly marketing budget by a month's new customers. Align the period and the unit before combining numbers.
  • Using revenue for LTV. Use contribution or gross profit, not revenue.
  • Loading central overhead onto one unit. Allocated costs can make a good store or route look bad.

Practise

1. A gym member pays $40 a month and costs $5 a month to serve. 4% of members leave each month. Winning a member costs $150. What are LTV and the LTV-to-CAC ratio?

Show the answer

Monthly contribution: $35. Average lifetime: 1 ÷ 0.04 = 25 months. LTV = $35 × 25 = $875. Ratio: $875 ÷ $150 ≈ 5.8 times, comfortably healthy.

2. In the delivery example, costs per order stay at $7.00 and the delivery fee at $2.00. What average order value makes contribution exactly zero?

Show the answer

Revenue is 25% × order value + $2.00. Set it equal to $7.00: 25% × order value = $5.00, so order value = $20. Below that, every order loses money, which is why apps use minimum orders and small-basket fees.

3. A coffee shop sells 500 cups a day at $4, 360 days a year. Ingredients and other variable costs are 35% of sales; its rent and staff cost $400k a year. Head office allocates it $80k of central costs. Should the chain close it?

Show the answer

Sales: 500 × $4 × 360 = $720k. Contribution: 65% × $720k = $468k. After its own costs: $468k − $400k = $68k. After the allocation it shows a $12k loss, but closing it would lose $68k a year that currently helps pay for head office, which would not shrink. Keep it open unless the site could be used for something better.

Where to practise next

See how business models shape the unit in how businesses make money, and how fixed costs change the picture in operating leverage. The LeafCart case is a pure unit economics problem, and the profitability framework shows where unit economics fit in a full case.
